sentences.text: Petra asked to be taught and her grandmother said no.
Not unkindly.
She said: "I can't teach it because nobody taught me.
I watched, and I got it wrong for about nine years, and then one year I got it right and I couldn't tell you what changed." "That's not helpful." "It isn't.
I know." Her grandmother was doing something at the sink.
"But if I make you a chart you'll read the chart and not the stag, and the chart will be wrong in a year that matters.
So no." What she did instead was better and much slower.
It was also, Petra realised at about thirty, the only way anybody has ever taught anybody anything difficult, and it is the method that no school has time for.
She started taking Petra with her.
That was all.
Three or four times a week, from April, they went up the top field or along the birches or down to the stream, and if the stag was there they looked at him, and Petra was asked one question.
*What's changed.* Not what does it mean.
Just what has changed.
For the first month Petra could not answer at all.
A stag is a stag; the antlers are complicated and they are also moving because he is moving, and they are usually a hundred metres away against a background of branches which are also complicated.
By June she could say *he's grown*.
This was received without comment, which was the system.
There was never any praise and there was never any correction.
Her grandmother would hear the answer, and nod, or not nod, and they would keep walking, and Petra would spend the next four days working out which it had been.
She learned things in a strange order.

She learned the light before she learned the antlers — that he was easiest to see in the hour before the sun went behind the ridge, and almost impossible at noon, and that this was not about brightness but about which way the shadows ran in the birches.
She learned that he had a place he stood and three places he might stand and that if he was in none of the four you would not find him that day and should go home.
She learned, in July, that he knew perfectly well they were there.
That was the one that took her a while.

He never fled and never approached and never fed while they were watching, and once, in the second week of July, he turned his head and looked directly at her grandmother for a period that Petra found extremely uncomfortable and that her grandmother met without any reaction at all.

"Does he know you?" "He knows there's two of us and there used to be one." By the end of July she could say *the right one's gone out and the left one's gone up*, which her grandmother received with a nod and no comment whatsoever.

By the following March — because it takes a year, and the antlers drop in the spring and grow again from nothing between April and August, and you cannot learn this thing in a season for the simple reason that there is only one of them per year — by the following March, Petra could look at a stag at ninety metres in poor light and say what was different from the week before.
The winter in between had been the hard part, and nobody had warned her about it.
The antlers come off in the spring.
She had known this in the way you know a fact.

She had not understood that it meant the stag she had spent five months learning would, in April, simply stop being the same object — that the whole structure she had been watching grow would drop off in a wood somewhere and a new one would start from two bare stumps.
She took it badly.
She said something at the kitchen table about all of it having been a waste, and her grandmother let her finish and then said: "You didn't learn the antlers.
You learnt to look." "That's a thing adults say." "It is," her grandmother agreed.
"It's also true, which is why they say it.
Go up on Thursday and tell me you can't find him against those birches in nine seconds flat.
You couldn't do that in April." Petra went up on the Thursday partly to prove her wrong.
She found him in about four seconds, in flat grey light, at over a hundred metres, standing in the third of his four places, and she stood there in the cold feeling extremely annoyed about it.
She still could not say what any of it meant.
"That's fine," said her grandmother.
"That's the whole of the first part and it takes most people three years."
